subject: art-design
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Analysing the work of artists and designers

questions.q: Which artist's 1872 painting 'Impression, Sunrise' gave the Impressionist movement its name?
questions.explain: The movement was named after Monet's 'Impression, Sunrise', originally a critic's mocking label.

questions.q: Cubism is most closely associated with which two artists?
questions.explain: Picasso and Braque developed Cubism together in the early 20th century.

questions.q: Andy Warhol, famous for his images of soup cans and celebrities, is a leading figure of which movement?
questions.explain: Warhol drew on mass-media and consumer imagery, a hallmark of Pop Art.

questions.q: Which best describes a key aim of Impressionist painters?
options: Capturing the fleeting effects of light and atmosphere with loose brushwork
Depicting dreams and the unconscious mind
Reducing objects to flat geometric shapes
Copying classical sculpture as accurately as possible
questions.explain: Impressionists often painted outdoors to record changing light and momentary impressions.

questions.q: The 'Surrealist Manifesto' of 1924 was written by which artist and poet?
questions.explain: André Breton authored the 1924 manifesto that defined Surrealism.

questions.q: Which characteristic is most typical of Cubist artworks?
options: Showing objects from several viewpoints at once using fragmented, geometric forms
Soft, blurred edges to capture sunlight
Realistic religious scenes with linear perspective
questions.explain: Cubism breaks subjects into planes and shows multiple viewpoints simultaneously.

questions.q: The Bauhaus, an influential design school founded in Germany in 1919, was established by whom?
questions.explain: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in 1919, uniting art, craft and design.

questions.q: Fauvism, led by Henri Matisse, is best known for which quality?
options: Bold, expressive and non-naturalistic use of colour
questions.explain: The Fauves used vivid, unrealistic colour for emotional and decorative effect.

questions.q: The formal elements of art include line, tone, colour, texture and which of the following?
questions.explain: Form (along with shape, pattern and space) is one of the formal elements used to analyse art.

questions.q: When analysing an artwork, what does the term 'composition' refer to?
options: The arrangement of the visual elements within the artwork
The price the artwork sold for
The date the artwork was made
questions.explain: Composition describes how elements are organised within the picture space.

questions.q: In the formal elements, what does 'tone' refer to?
options: The lightness and darkness of a colour or surface
The roughness or smoothness of a surface
questions.explain: Tone describes how light or dark an area is, helping to create form and depth.

questions.q: In art analysis, the term 'media' (or medium) refers to what?
options: The materials and tools used to make the work
questions.explain: Media means the materials, such as oil paint, charcoal or clay, used to create art.

questions.q: A student notices strong contrasts between light and dark areas creating a dramatic, three-dimensional effect in a portrait. Which technique is being used?
questions.explain: Chiaroscuro is the use of strong tonal contrast to model form and create drama.

questions.q: Why is understanding the historical context of an artwork useful when analysing it?
options: It helps explain the artist's influences, purpose and meaning
It tells you exactly how much the work is worth
It guarantees the work is a masterpiece
It removes the need to look at the artwork itself
questions.explain: Knowing the context reveals why and how a work was made, deepening the analysis.

questions.q: In a sketchbook, what does an 'artist study' usually involve?
options: Recreating part of an artist's work to understand their techniques
Writing an essay about the artist's life only
Buying a print of the artwork
questions.explain: An artist study copies and explores a work to learn about its methods and media.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of annotation in a sketchbook?
options: To record and explain thoughts, analysis and creative decisions
To make the page look decorative
To fill empty space with words
To list the cost of materials
questions.explain: Annotation documents your thinking, analysis and reasoning behind the work.

questions.q: Which annotation shows the strongest critical response to an artwork?
options: The artist's jagged lines and dark tones create a sense of tension that I find unsettling
I like this picture a lot
This must have taken a long time to make
questions.explain: A strong response uses subject vocabulary and gives a personal opinion supported by evidence.

questions.q: When recording a response to a landscape painted in soft, muted colours, which word best describes the mood likely created?
questions.explain: Soft, muted colours typically create a calm, tranquil atmosphere.

questions.q: A well-recorded critical response should above all include which of the following?
options: Personal opinions supported by evidence from the artwork
Only a summary of the artist's biography
A single word saying whether you like it
A copy of the gallery label with no comment
questions.explain: Critical responses combine personal judgement with reasons drawn from the work itself.

questions.q: A designer creates a poster using bold flat colours, comic-style Ben-Day dots and imagery borrowed from advertising. Which movement most strongly influences this work?
questions.explain: Flat colour, Ben-Day dots and mass-media imagery are signatures of Pop Art.
